title: Evaluating QAOA expectation values can be as hard as counting optimal solutions
abstract: Evaluating expectation values is a critical task for variational quantum eigensolvers, and for parameterized quantum circuits and other quantum algorithms more generally. We consider the well-studied case of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for the MaxCut problem. Recent work of Wang et al. [arXiv:2511.20212] showed this task to be NP-hard in general for any QAOA depth $p\geq 2$, complementing past results showing efficiently computable formulas for $p=1$ with arbitrary problem graphs. We sharpen this dichotomy showing that for $p\geq 2$ exact or exponentially precise cost expectation value evaluation is #P-hard under deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. Hardness at $p\geq 2$ is shown to remain even for evaluating single pairwise correlators $\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle $, as well as for highly restricted sets of algorithm parameters. Our proof refines the NP-hardness construction of Wang et al. that recovers the maximum cut value from the largest exponent of a QAOA Laurent polynomial, utilizing a distinct and simpler construction that extracts a value proportional to the total number of maximum cuts, in addition to the optimal cut value. Thus we show that the QAOA expectation value hardness transition from $p=1$ to $p=2$ is not only from tractability to optimization hardness, but to that of counting optimal solutions. As an application we show our results imply analogous hardness results for computing gradients and Hessians of QAOA circuits.
summary: This paper rigorously proves that evaluating expectation values for QAOA circuits at depth $p \geq 2$ is computationally intractable, specifically showing it is \#P-hard. By constructing specialized graph gadgets, the authors reduce the problem of counting maximum cuts to calculating a specific coefficient in the QAOA's resulting Laurent polynomial. This establishes a significant complexity barrier for variational quantum algorithms.
main_problem: The core problem is determining the computational complexity of evaluating expectation values for variational quantum algorithms, specifically QAOA applied to MaxCut.
main_result: The authors prove that for fixed depth $p \geq 2$, evaluating these expectation values (and related quantities like gradients/Hessians) is \#P-hard, meaning it is as hard as counting optimal solutions.
method: The hardness proof refines previous work by constructing specialized 'counting gadgets' within the QAOA framework. This allows mapping the problem of counting maximum cuts ($\#	ext{MC}(G)$) to the coefficient extraction from a Laurent polynomial derived from the expectation value.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) applied to finding the MaxCut of a graph $G$. The system is described by cost and mixer Hamiltonians, leading to quantum states $|\psi_p(\gamma,  eta)angle$ at depth $p$.
key_observables: The primary observable is the cost expectation value $F_p(G; \gamma,  eta) = \langle\psi_p|C_G|\psi_pangle$, and also single pairwise correlators $\langle Z_r Z_s angle$.
important_parameters: The depth parameter $p$ is critical: $p=1$ is tractable ($\in 	ext{FP}$), while fixed $p \geq 2$ exhibits \#P-hardness.
main_assumptions: The hardness results apply to worst-case families of graphs and require evaluating the expectation value with exponential precision ($\epsilon = 2^{-cN}$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a balanced counting gadget for $K_3$, demonstrating how the number of maximum cuts in the constructed graph relates directly to the original graph's count.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes tractability for $p=1$ (Chunk 4). It then builds upon this by introducing specialized gadgets and mathematical tools (Laurent polynomials) to prove that exact evaluation becomes \#P-hard for fixed $p \geq 2$ (Chunks 1 & 2). Finally, it extends the hardness result to computing derivatives like gradients and Hessians (Chunk 3).
why_interesting: This work provides a strong theoretical barrier, suggesting that simulating or optimizing complex quantum algorithms beyond shallow circuits requires computational resources equivalent to solving hard counting problems.
